newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. bars Iraqi rental of Turkish TV satellite.
newsitem.headline: U.N. bars Iraqi rental of Turkish TV satellite.

text.p: A U.N. sanctions committee turned down a Turkish request on Monday to be allowed to rent Iraq a satellite transponder band to broadcast television programmes seen within Iraq as well as by its neighbours and in Western Europe.
"We could not agree because the rendering of services of this kind was not considered a civilian need," committee chairman Tono Eitel of Germany said.
He was speaking to reporters after a closed-door meeting of the Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee, which has the same 15-nation membership as the council itself.

The request was for the Turkish Telekom Administration to rent Iraq a transponder band from Turksat 1-C satellite, with payments to be made in advance in U.S. currency and in cash. The deal, for which no cost was given, would not have involved the shipment to Iraq of any equipment or spare parts.

Iraq has been under strict U.N. sanctions since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The only exceptions are for food, medicine and other humanitarian goods, which the sanctions committee monitors closely.

The committee also declined to give blanket advance approval to a Jordanian request for permission for Royal Jordanian Airline to make one or more regular weekly flights between Amman and Baghdad to carry U.N. personnel and for humanitarian purposes.
But Eitel said such flights would be considered "case by case, and hopefully approved."

Jordan said the flights would be used to carry U.N. observers and other staff to and from Iraq; elderly and sick passengers who would otherwise have to drive across the desert to and from Baghdad; pilgrims travelling to Moslem shrines in Iraq, and shipments of food and medicine.

The committee was also briefed by a U.N. official on the status of a plan concluded last May to enable Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over six months to buy food, medicines and other humanitarian supplies.
Eitel said there had been no change since last week when the Security Council was told that conditions were not yet ripe for the plan to be implemented.
Still at issue were the number of U.N. inspectors needed to oversee operations and their freedom of movement.
"The Iraqis want some advance notice (of their movements), possibly one or two weeks. Which is of course difficult, to put it mildly, impossible to accept, to put it more correctly," Eitel said.
But the U.N. official who briefed the committee said Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was "confident that all the questions still under discussion with the Iraqi side would be solved."

The U.N. official said it was too early to assess the effect on the oil-for-food plan of the recent upsurge of fighting between Kurdish factions in northern Iraq which resulted in the recapture over the weekend by the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan of the city of Sulaimaniya from the Kurdistan Democratic Party.
